content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors discuss the relation between the conditional action similarity of agents and their respective ZSC performance. Unsurprisingly, agents that are trained with a partner similar to the unseen agent perform better with the unseen agent.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths
* This paper focuses on a very important problem, currently at the forefront of MARL research. 
* Investigating the behavior of agents is not done enough and is very helpful for the community. 
* For these two reasons I wanted to like the paper, but found the actual analysis problematic (see negatives). 

### Weaknesses:
* The biggest issue with this work is that the main finding is trivial and already known. To quote the authors themselves, "if the ZSC partner is similar to an agent's training partner, the agent might cooperate with this unseen partner well". This is essentially saying that an agent will perform well with another if it has already trained with a similar agent, which is basically self-play. Further, it has been shown in many works, such as in the original ZS paper by Hu et al. that conditional action similarity is related to cross play. This is essentially shown in Figure 5 of the OP paper, and actually it is shown better there because there is more interpretability regarding conventions in Hanabi. Showing this relationship quantitatively may constitute a workshop paper, but we certainly don't need to name it "CPSTT". If the authors wish to pursue this agenda further, it might be interesting to be a bit more rigorous beyond pointing to a known correlation. 
* Section 4 is quite strange. It is just two paragraphs discussing how intra algorithm cross play could be different to inter algorithm cross play, when really we should be looking at the relative performance vs. self-play here. For example the authors make a big point about how intra alg XP is worse for VDN than when it is paired with SAD, but SAD is a much stronger agent, so this is quite obvious? Essentially what this is saying is "When you partner an agent with a stronger one in a cooperative game they do better", which is trivial. I think it would be best to just delete this section. 
* The authors do not properly understand the ZSC problem, stating in the second paragraph of the paper "where the agents must coordinate with unfamilar partners they have not seen before". Indeed, in Hu et al it is instead defined as the performance across seeds of the same algorithm. In the paper the authors define both "intra" and "inter" ZSC. The ZSC problem is typically the "intra" version discussed, while the "inter" problem is known as "Ad Hoc Teamplay". Please see Hu et al and Bard et al for this distinction. 
* The idea that policy similarity and ZSC performance are decoupled is again obvious. Consider an agent that takes random actions, if we clone this agent, then it will have a high CPSTT with its clone, but both will achieve a very low ZSC score. Of course an algorithm like SAD will outperform this, because it will have a lower CPSTT and a higher ZSC score. This paper is essentially putting the cart before the horse. 
* The idea of SBRT is essentially just adding exploration noise, and maybe a novelty bonus to the current agent. Is this correct?

Minor issues:
* Many grammatical mistakes, including in the very first line: 
  - first line of the paper: "Over these years" -> "Over the years", but you probably mean "In recent years". 
  - intro: "between cross play score" -> "between the cross play score".
  - Apostrophes in latex are done incorrectly e.g. `blue' on p4.
* The over-use of acronyms makes it quite hard to read, which is definitely not ideal in the days of 4k ICLR submissions. 
* Correct me if I am wrong but AUX stands for auxiliary loss right? What is the baseline method it is combined with? Shouldn't it be "SAD+AUX" as in previous works?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The idea is largely clear, aside from over-use of long acronyms to describe simple things. The novelty is essentially zero because other papers like Hu et al have shown action similarity is related to ZSC.
content.summary_of_the_review: Given many of these results were known before, the paper does not add anything to the community so I recommend rejection. The analyses may form the basis of an interesting paper in the future, but at present it is superficial and largely trivial.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.title: Response Part 1
content.comment:
Thanks for your suggestions which help us improve our work. Below we address your concerns in detail.

**[Weakness 1]The biggest issue with this work is that the main finding is trivial and already known. To quote the authors themselves, "if the ZSC partner is similar to an agent's training partner, the agent might cooperate with this unseen partner well". This is essentially saying that an agent will perform well with another if it has already trained with a similar agent, which is basically self-play. Further, it has been shown in many works, such as in the original ZS paper by Hu et al. that conditional action similarity is related to cross play. This is essentially shown in Figure 5 of the OP paper, and actually it is shown better there because there is more interpretability regarding conventions in Hanabi. Showing this relationship quantitatively may constitute a workshop paper, but we certainly don't need to name it "CPSTT". If the authors wish to pursue this agenda further, it might be interesting to be a bit more rigorous beyond pointing to a known correlation.**

We admit that the idea "if the ZSC partner is similar to an agent's training partner, the agent might cooperate with this unseen partner well" is intuitive and is revealed in earlier works. However, our first contribution is to deeply study this correlation and find a surprisingly strong linear correlation, which we believe is valuable. Based on this correlation, we propose a new metric as well as a new training scheme. Current work on zero-shot coordination mainly focuses on making agents learn intrinsic rules of cooperative games or avoiding special conventions between training partners, and we believe our findings and successful attempt at SBRT can provide a new perspective for research in this area.

**[Weakness 3]The authors do not properly understand the ZSC problem, stating in the second paragraph of the paper "where the agents must coordinate with unfamilar partners they have not seen before". Indeed, in Hu et al it is instead defined as the performance across seeds of the same algorithm. In the paper the authors define both "intra" and "inter" ZSC. The ZSC problem is typically the "intra" version discussed, while the "inter" problem is known as "Ad Hoc Teamplay". Please see Hu et al and Bard et al for this distinction.**

Thank you for the suggestion. We have carefully reread [1] and found that the comment conflicts with some statements in [1]. Hu et al.[1] do not define ZSC as intra-algorithm cross-play. The first sentence of Abstract in [1] is “We consider the problem of zero-shot coordination - constructing AI agents that can coordinate with novel partners they have not seen before”, and we follow this definition. 

Besides, Hu et al. mention the difference between ad-hoc teamplay and ZSC in Sec 2.2 of [1]: “Ad-hoc teamwork differs from the zero-shot coordination problem in that it is typically framed as a learning problem of learning the policies/capabilities of other agents during interaction whereas the pure zero-shot coordination scenario is one where there is no time to update a fixed policy that is constructed during training.” 

From the above statements, inter-algorithm cross-play and intra-algorithm cross-play both are zero-shot coordination and not ad-hoc teamwork. However, when conducting experiments (Sec.6.4 of [1]), Hu et al. state that “Clearly, if independent training runs (“seeds”) from the same training method fail to coordinate with each other at test time it is unlikely they will coordinate with agents optimized by through a different process, let alone humans”, and therefore only test intra-algorithm cross-play. Following this setting, some researchers also use intra-algorithm cross-play to measure ZSC performance, and maybe that’s why the reviewer thinks “intra-algorithm cross-play=ZSC”.

The concept of intra-algorithm cross-play and inter-algorithm cross-play is also not proposed by us. It is defined in [2]. We mention this paper when we give definitions of inter-algorithm cross-play in Sec.3.1. Additionally, both [2] and our paper find that simply conducting intra-algorithm cross-play to measure ZSC performance is not enough. The definition of ZSC is “coordinate with novel partners they have not seen before”, so only choosing agents trained with the same framework as testing partners seems less convincing.  Our results present in Table 1 also confirm this point: intra-algorithm cross-play scores cannot fully represent the ZSC performance of models. 

[1]Hu, Hengyuan, et al. "“Other-Play” for Zero-Shot Coordination." *International Conference on Machine Learning*. PMLR, 2020.

[2]Lucas, Keane, and Ross E. Allen. "Any-Play: An Intrinsic Augmentation for Zero-Shot Coordination." *Proceedings of the 21st International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems*. 2022.

content.title: Response part 2
content.comment:
**[Weakness 2]Section 4 is quite strange. It is just two paragraphs discussing how intra algorithm cross play could be different to inter algorithm cross play, when really we should be looking at the relative performance vs. self-play here. For example the authors make a big point about how intra alg XP is worse for VDN than when it is paired with SAD, but SAD is a much stronger agent, so this is quite obvious? Essentially what this is saying is "When you partner an agent with a stronger one in a cooperative game they do better", which is trivial. I think it would be best to just delete this section.**

We are aware that Sec.4 may be a little confusing and make some adjustments in the updated version. We also present self-play scores in Sec.4 according to your suggestions. The original purpose of Sec.4 is to show that cross-play scores vary a lot, so it may not be suitable enough to measure a model’s ZSC performance only by averaged cross-play scores with some specific testing partners.

**[Weakness 4]The idea that policy similarity and ZSC performance are decoupled is again obvious. Consider an agent that takes random actions, if we clone this agent, then it will have a high CPSTT with its clone, but both will achieve a very low ZSC score. Of course an algorithm like SAD will outperform this, because it will have a lower CPSTT and a higher ZSC score. This paper is essentially putting the cart before the horse.**

It is true that cross-play scores are indeed not necessarily related to policy similarity between one agent and its partner. If a random agent  has a similar policy to its partner, the cooperation is not guaranteed to be good. However, this does not conflict with our findings. Cross-play scores are strongly linearly correlated with the conditional policy similarity between an agent’s training partner and testing partner (i.e. CPSTT), and we give definitions of training partner **πp** and testing partner **πo** in Eq.(1) and Eq.(2). Therefore, when we mention that “cross-play scores are linearly correlated with CPSTT”, we assume the agents are well-trained and can cooperate with the training partners well.

**[Weakness 5]The idea of SBRT is essentially just adding exploration noise, and maybe a novelty bonus to the current agent. Is this correct?**

The operation of SBRT may seem simple, however, the core idea of it is motivated by our finding that cross-play scores are linearly correlated with CPSTT. As is stated in the first paragraph of Sec.6, “cross-play scores can be increased in two ways based on CPSTT, and the second one is to improve cross-play scores while CPSTT is fixed”. The purpose of perturbing the training partner’s actions is to manually create **πa** s.t. **CPSTT_π (πp, πa) = α.** Therefore, the idea of SBRT is largely different from exploration noise in RL. Actually, SBRT is inspired by robust RL techniques, which actively create unfavorable conditions during training to obtain a more robust agent. Besides, we hope our successful attempt at combining ZSC with robust RL can provide a new perspective on ZSC research.

**[Minor issues 1]Many grammatical mistakes, including in the very first line**

Thanks for your suggestions, and we correct them in the updated version.

**[Minor issues 2]The over-use of acronyms makes it quite hard to read, which is definitely not ideal in the days of 4k ICLR submissions.**

We are sorry for the inconvenience and remove unnecessary acronyms in the updated version.

**[Minor issues 3]Correct me if I am wrong but AUX stands for auxiliary loss right? What is the baseline method it is combined with? Shouldn't it be "SAD+AUX" as in previous works?**

Thanks for pointing this out. AUX stands for “SAD+AUX”, and we add descriptions in the updated version.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper describes the problem of inter-algorithm cross-play, i.e. how well agents from different algorithms and training seeds, cooperate.
The authors hypothesize that the similarity between an agent's training partner and test partner decreases with cross-play performance.
They show that this hypothesis is true, and present a training scheme to increase the cross-play performance. The training scheme perturbs the training partner's actions with three alternative methods, all of which actions are chosen from a policy trained by another algorithm.
Their opinion is that the cross-play score is not reliable, because it varies greatly between agents from different algorithms.

content.title: Response part 1
content.comment:
We appreciate the detailed comment and in-depth suggestions. We are aware of your concerns and address them in detail:

**[Weakness 1]They focus on self-play (SP) agents, while SP-trained agents are not necessarily good at solving zero-shot coordination (ZSC) problems. An example is presented by Hu et al. (2020) with the lever game. Since: "self-play agents typically construct ‘inhuman’ strategies" and "SP may reach inefficient equilibria".**

SP-trained agents may not be good at solving ZSC problems, however, SP is the most efficient way to train agents (as a comparison, population-based training requires much more computing resources). Therefore, proposing light-weight schemes to improve the ZSC performance of SP-trained agents is also important. For example, the paper[1] mentioned in this comment also proposes methods to improve SP-trained agents’ ZSC performance. 

[1]Hu, Hengyuan, et al. "“Other-Play” for Zero-Shot Coordination." *International Conference on Machine Learning*. PMLR, 2020.

**[Weakness 2]They show a high correlation between cross-play (XP) and their CPSTT (Conditional Policy Similarity between an agent’s Training partner and Testing partner). The result of SP-marl is a joint policy that achieves maximal return, converging to one in which both agents' policies act exactly as seen during training. So, it is obvious that if the policy of an agent's partner is very different from its training partner, it cannot obtain a maximal score.**

We agree with you that “it is obvious that if the policy of an agent's partner is very different from its training partner, it cannot obtain a maximal score.” This is intuitive and becomes our motivation, as is mentioned in paragraph 3 of Sec.1. To investigate what exactly this correlation is, we define CPSTT and find a strong linear correlation between CPSTT and cross-play scores. Based on it, we design a new criterion to help better evaluate ZSC performance (If one model achieves higher cross-play scores than another one given an arbitrary CPSTT, then it is considered better.) and propose SBRT to improve agents’ ZSC performance. 

**[Weakness 3]Does the similarity measure (equation (3)) only apply to deterministic policies?**

It applies to deterministic policies as well as stochastic policies. For example, given an action trajectory **τ** and two stochastic policies **πa, πb.** Suppose there are three possible actions **a1, a2, a3.** Then 

P(πa(τ)=πb(τ))=πa(a1|τ)*πb(a1|τ)+πa(a2|τ)*πb(a2|τ)+πa(a3|τ)*πb(a3|τ)

In our experiments, we use deterministic policies, for they are better than stochastic policies [1] in Hanabi.

[1]Hu, Hengyuan, and Jakob N. Foerster. "Simplified Action Decoder for Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning." *International Conference on Learning Representations*
. 2019.

**[Weakness 4.1]The experiments show that IQL's correlation coefficient is the lowest and AUX's highest. What is a possible explanation of this result?**

Sometimes the action difference is not important, which means if the testing partner acts differently from the testing partner, it is OK, while sometimes the action difference is vital. We suspect that for AUX agents, the action differences are mainly “important”, so the correlation between CPSTT and cross-play scores is strong; while for IQL agents, there are some “unimportant differences”, so the correlation between CPSTT and cross-play scores is weaker. 

**[Weakness 4.2]Does equation (5) say that models can be compared on their XP scores, given that they have the *exact* same similarity score, so x is not a value in R, because if it is, it would be hard to have the same values?**

①Here x represents CPSTT, which ranges between 0 and 1

②It is hard to precisely calculate J^π_s(x) given an arbitrary x, for the testing partner set is finite. Therefore, we use a linear fit function to approximate it with enough XP results.

content.title: Reponse part 2
content.comment:
**[Weakness 5]How should one choose the set of algorithms in SBRT? Robustness increases with the size of the set of policies, but also with the dissimilarity of the training algorithms for the policies.**

We show how different implementation options affect the performance of SBRT. In particular, we present the performance of different types of SBRT (worst/best/random alternative action) in Appendix B and conclude that random alternative action is the best.  Besides, we show how different α_r (i.e. how frequently we perturb the partner action) affects the performance in Sec. 6.3, and find that α_r=0.8 is the best.

**[Weakness 6]The conclusion says that XP scores are unreliable, yet, CPSTT is highly correlated with XP. Is CPSTT also unreliable then?**

We are sorry for the imprecise statement. The XP score of two kinds of models is reliable, which directly reflects how well they cooperate; what is unreliable is only using averaged XP scores to judge a model’s ZSC performance. The reason is that XP scores are highly correlated with CPSTT, and the choice of testing partners will heavily influence XP scores. Thanks for pointing this out, and we adjust related statements in the conclusion  to avoid misunderstanding. 

**[Clarity]If the trajectories contain continuous valued states/actions, can the comparison (equation (4)) between π1 and π2 be made on a trajectory τi with i∈[0,n]?**

Our definition of policy similarity is based on discrete actions. It can be intuitively extended to continuous scenarios by replacing P(πa(τ)=πb(τ)) with -(πa(τ)-πb(τ))^2. However, there are currently no suitable continuous scenarios to study ZSC, making it hard to validate the practicality of this definition.

**[Novelty and relevance 1]As mentioned previously, how relevant are agents that are trained with SBRT if the result are SP-trained agents?** 

We present the SBRT agents’ CPSTT in Fig. 3.

**[Novelty and relevance 2]Hu et al. 2020 state that ZSC coordination games can often not be solved by SP. How relevant are inter-cross-play algorithms for developing AI agents that can cooperate with humans? For example, the set of algorithms can have very "inhuman" strategies.**

This is a good question, for the policy of humans may be quite different from that of trained AI. However, we fail to get human data in this task, and we will continue trying to solve this problem in the future.

**[Practicality]How does their SBRT scale (computation) with the number of agents and state/action space?**

There are three types of SBRT. Random alternative action simply makes the partner chooses a random action, and requires almost no computation. Best alternative action and worst alternative action make the partner chooses alternative actions based on the Q-function, which in our implementation outputs the Q-values of all feasible actions. Therefore, these two types of SBRT only require an additional max or min operation when modifying the training partner’s actions, which is also fast and convenient.

**[Originality]How different is their SBRT from population-based training? And, can they formulate the solution or outcome of the policies that result from training under SBRT?**

SBRT and population-based training both try to make agents learn with more diverse partners. SBRT achieves this by perturbing the training partner’s actions according to a predefined CPSTT, which is convenient. In comparison, population-based training requires training a population of agents, which needs more computation resources. We also notice that SBRT can be applied to population-based training, (an intuitive approach is to perturb the actions of training partners in population-based training) which is a potential future work direction.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for your approval of our findings, and we summarize our response to address your concerns:

**[Weakness 1]SBRT gets strong performance, but it falls short with AUX, which is already the highest-performing algorithm, so that was disappointing to see.**

Actually, AUX+SBRT is not good measured with traditional metrics (simply using the averaged intra-algorithm cross-play scores and inter-algorithm cross-play scores to judge one model’s ZSC performance). However, as is shown in Fig.1, the cross-play scores vary a lot and are highly related to CPSTT, so it may not be suitable enough to only rely on cross-play scores to evaluate ZSC performance. As the example mentioned in Sec.1 paragraph 4 , “if type-A models have high cross-play scores with type-C models while type-B models have low cross-play scores with type-C models, it does not necessarily mean that the ZSC performance of type-B models is worse compared to type-A models. The reason may be that CPSTT between type-A models and type-C models is higher.” 

Considering the strong linear correlation between CPSTT and cross-play scores, we propose a new criterion to evaluate ZSC performance, that is if one model achieves higher cross-play scores than another one given an arbitrary CPSTT, then it is considered better. And SBRT indeed improves AUX’s performance measured by this new metric.

The reason why AUX+SBRT gets lower cross-play scores is that SBRT lowers CPSTT of AUX models, which is visualized in Figure 3.

**[Weakness 2] There also appear to be a number of hyperparameters and implementation options in SBRT so I'm concerned the authors might have found settings that are overfit to Hanabi.**

Actually there are only two implementation options for SBRT. ①How to choose a_alt (there are three options)②How to set α_r (α_r∈(0,1)). Besides, we give analysis in Section 6.3 and Appendix B to illustrate how different options affect the results. Results show that random alternative action and α_r=0.2 are the best settings.

**[Clarity, Quality, Novelty And Reproducibility 1] CPSTT is defined multiple times in the paper. Defining it the first time it is introduced is sufficient.**

Thank you for your suggestion and we fix this problem in the updated version.

**[Clarity, Quality, Novelty And Reproducibility 2] It's not clear how to read Table 2**

Table 2 shows how accurate our estimation is. In particular, we test multiple combinations of models. For each combination, we run the test (which shows cross-play scores and CPSTT) for 100 times, and get 100 sets of results. Then we calculate the Std/Mean (i.e. coefficients of variation) of the results to see if our estimation is accurate enough. (Mean can be treated as the true value and Std can be treated as MSE of the estimation). It can be seen that the standard deviation is quite small compared to the mean for both cross-play score and CPSTT, which confirms the accuracy of our estimation. In the updated version, we adjust our presentation to make it easier for readers to read Table 2.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors address the problem of measuring Zero Shot Coordination, an important problem in multi-agent RL. The paper defines the Conditional Policy Similarity between an agent’s Training partner and Testing partner (CPSTT) to help better understand the relationship between cross-play scores and zero-shot coordination performance. As the name implies, CPSTT is the expected probability that an agent's partner during test time performs the same action the agent's training partner would have. The paper finds that high CPSTT correlates strongly with high cross-play scores without necessarily implying good zero-shot coordination. Therefore, the authors propose a new criterion for evaluating zero shot coordination - higher cross play score given the same CPSTT. The authors also propose Similarity Based Robust Training (SBRT), a training scheme which perturbs a training partner's actions to achieve a certain CPSTT, and find that SBRT improves zero-shot coordination in four MARL frameworks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1) The proposed metric CPSTT is clearly and intuitively motivated by the observations in Section 4, and SBRT is in turn a reasonable application of CPSTT to agent training. The experiments and ablations clearly address the questions I had while reading the paper. 

2) The experimental performance of SBRT is largely convincing, and uses a suitable baseline. 

Weaknesses:

1) Although Hanabi is a standard environment for evaluating cooperation and coordination, it would be nice to see results in other environments as well. 

2) Intuitively, not all different actions are equal - some may simply be a reordering of the same steps, while others may be moving towards an entirely different goal. As an adversarial example, if the task were to navigate to two separate corners of a gridworld, a stationary partner would have the same CPSTT as a test partner that simply prefers a different corner than the training partner, but these partners would have drastically different cross-play scores. 

Questions:

2) Which Q-function is used to select the best and worst alternative action? 

3) Is $\pi_a$ or \pi_p$ used when computing CPSTT while using SBRT?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity - The paper is well presented. The observed problem with cross-play is clearly laid-out. The related works section does a good job providing background for ZSC and related metrics. 

Quality - The paper is overall of high quality. The experiments are well laid out and the results are convincing. The paper is well written and polished. 

Originality - The paper proposes a new approach to considering and measuring zero shot coordination, which is intuitive but not clearly defined in previous works, as well as a novel method for training.
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors provide a novel and well motivated method for evaluating Zero Shot Coordination, an important problem in cooperative multi-agent RL, and experimentally demonstrate improved performance using their training method. However, it's unclear to me how well this method generalizes to tasks besides Hanabi.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for acknowledging our work, and we will reply to your concerns below.

**[Weakness 1]Although Hanabi is a standard environment for evaluating cooperation and coordination, it would be nice to see results in other environments as well.**

We choose to test in Hanabi because it has very high requirements for cooperation (agents must share their intentions as well as infer their partners’ intentions), making zero-shot coordination difficult. Consequently, works in this area mainly conduct experiments in Hanabi [1-5]. 

[1]Hu, Hengyuan, et al. "“Other-Play” for Zero-Shot Coordination." *International Conference on Machine Learning*. PMLR, 2020.

[2]Lupu, Andrei, et al. "Trajectory diversity for zero-shot coordination." *International Conference on Machine Learning*. PMLR, 2021.

[3]Hu, Hengyuan, et al. "Off-belief learning." *International Conference on Machine Learning*. PMLR, 2021.

[4]Cui, Brandon, et al. "K-level Reasoning for Zero-Shot Coordination in Hanabi." *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems* 34 (2021): 8215-8228.

[5]Lucas, Keane, and Ross E. Allen. "Any-Play: An Intrinsic Augmentation for Zero-Shot Coordination." *Proceedings of the 21st International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems*. 2022.

**[Weakness 2]Intuitively, not all different actions are equal - some may simply be a reordering of the same steps, while others may be moving towards an entirely different goal. As an adversarial example, if the task were to navigate to two separate corners of a gridworld, a stationary partner would have the same CPSTT as a test partner that simply prefers a different corner than the training partner, but these partners would have drastically different cross-play scores.**

This is an interesting point. It is true sometimes the difference in actions is important and sometimes not. However, it is almost impossible to precisely measure this kind of difference. Besides, our proposed policy similarity is easy-to-estimate and the cross-play score has a strong linear correlation with CPSTT.  Therefore, our definition for policy similarity is practical and meaningful even though it does not take the inequity of actions into account.

**[Question 1]Which Q-function is used to select the best and worst alternative action？**

In SBRT, we modify an agent’s training partner’s policy during training to help the agent better adapt to unexpected partner behavior. Therefore, we use the training partner’s Q-function to select the best and worst alternative action.

**[Question 2]Is πa or \pi_p$ used when computing CPSTT while using SBRT?**

We use πp to calculate CPSTT for SBRT models. During our training, we construct πa by randomly perturbing πp.
